1.52.m: The twice-born said: / "O Viṣṇu, how was there a blow from a stake on the body of the sage Māṇḍavya, / and how was there leprosy on the body of the devoted wife's husband?"
Hari said: / "Out of childishness, not thinking, Māṇḍavya inserted a blade of grass / into the abdomen of a cricket, and out of delusion he let it go.
By the fault of that censure, and by [the decree of] Dharma the knower, / day and night severe distress was endured by that twice-born man.
However, by that absorption, the distress caused by the stake was not felt, / nor all the hardship, by the sage, owing to intense practice of yoga.
From the slaying of a brāhmaṇa, on account of uncontrolled senses, / foul-smelling leprosy arose on the body of the leper, O best of the twice-born.
Formerly four virgin maidens were given by him to a brāhmaṇa, / and three maidens, O brāhmaṇa; therefore he had a devoted wife.
And on account of her, he would attain equality with me. / Whence is there any wonder in this? Know the ancient action!"
The twice-born said: / "Certainly heaven belongs to him who guides a faithful woman; / as this story [shows], O Lord, auspiciousness is wished for all."
Hari said: / "There are some dutiful women who give all their possessions to a man; / yet even toward one who should not be protected, one should not hold [desire] even in mind.
No one is unpleasant to women, nor is anyone truly dear; / like cattle in a forest seeking fresh grass, they crave ever new [men].
Even a man devoid of wealth, deformed, bereft of virtues, / of low birth, and a servant, a passionate woman truly resorts to.
Abandoning a husband endowed with virtues, well-born, very wealthy, / handsome, and skilled in love-making, a woman may resort to a base man.
Know the narrative of the conversation between Umā and Nārada, O earthly god, / by which, O twice-born, the various conduct of women is fully known.
By nature, O brāhmaṇa, the sage Nārada was eager to understand the universe; / having reflected in his own mind, he then went to the excellent Mount Kailāsa.
On the snowy mountain where the abode of the Bull-bannered [Śiva] is established, / that great-souled sage bowed down and asked Pārvatī:
"O goddess, I wish to know the wicked behaviour of women; / through curiosity, the conduct of wives is observed by you.
You know truly the inner heart of all women; / therefore tell me, who am humble and ignorant in all these matters."
The goddess said: / "The mind of young women always rests upon a man, without a doubt, / whether in this suitable union, or whether joined or unjoined."
Upon seeing a well-dressed man, whether a brother or a son, / a woman's womb becomes moist—truly, truly, O Nārada.
There is no place, there is no moment, there is no male suitor; / by that [alone], O Nārada, women's fidelity arises.
Woman is like a pot of ghee, man is like a burning coal; / therefore, one should never place ghee and fire in the same spot.
Just as a driver brings an elephant in rut under his control / by means of the hook and mallet, so too is a woman's protector.
Her father protects her in childhood, her husband protects her in youth, / and her sons [protect her] in old age: a woman does not deserve independence.
Therefore, through the absence of independence and of her own free will, / a steadfast noble woman, when solicited by a man through instigation, becomes unchaste.
Just as cooked food, through lack of protection, falls under the sway of dogs and crows, / so indeed a young woman, through wantonness, goes to wickedness.
Then her family becomes corrupted through association with her; / that one who is born from another's seed is indeed a mixture of castes.
The sinful illegitimate child of mixed caste surely dwells in hell; / [then] all of them, having gone into the species of worms, are born again on the surface of the earth.
Then, O joy of the twice-born, the family is brought to the status of a barbarian; / since the ruin of a lineage results, one should not keep a wicked woman.
That lowest of men who, knowing the fault of women, pardons [it], / remains in the terrible Raurava hell together with his ancestors.
One woman ruins a family, another elevates a family; / therefore, with every effort, a wise man should marry a well-born woman.
An equal woman stands keeping both families united; / a virtuous wife saves the lineages, a wicked woman certainly brings them down.
Heaven and the family, purity and disgrace, fame and ill repute, / son, daughter, and friend in worldly existence are said to depend upon a wife.
Therefore, a wise man should marry one or a second woman; / but she who is taken for offspring or out of desire is fraught with many faults.
And that husband who does not approach his wife when she has bathed after menstruation, / is a slayer of a brahmin, a slayer of an embryo, and goes to a wretched destination.
That evil-doer who, having made a virtuous wife unfortunate out of delusion, abandons her, / goes to hell after experiencing the sin equal to slaying her.
Having abducted a woman, a man goes to the family of a Cāṇḍāla; / likewise, through the abandonment of a woman, a man is born fallen.
Placing a woman on his shoulders, he dwells for a long time in the city of Yama; / feces and urine constantly fall upon his head.
In this way the evil-minded one carries the burden for thousands of years; / then, for as many years as there are body hairs, he goes to Raurava.
Having passed through [births] among worms, he then attains human status; / and then, because of former sin, he incurs strife and sorrow.
Having obtained three such births, a man is freed from the sin; / but that deceitful woman, having experienced hell for that time, becomes a female crow.
Having experienced the hell of leftover food, she becomes a widow among humans. / Furthermore, that man who goes to an outcaste woman, a barbarian woman, or a Pulkasa woman,
having suffered twice, thrice, or four times over as a deceitful sinner there, / [or he who] goes to his mother, his teacher's wife, a brahmin woman, a queen,
or any other wife of his lord, goes to non-rebirth [in a good state]; / [or he who goes to] his sister, his son's wife, and likewise his daughter, his daughter-in-law,
his paternal uncle's wife, his maternal aunt, and likewise his paternal aunt, / or other women such as his mother's sister—having gone to them, there is no expiation.
He becomes a slayer of a brahmin, blind, and falls into dumbness of speech; / born deaf in his ears, he falls; there is no expiation.
Having spoken very excessive obscenity entirely on account of a woman, / the twice-born said: "Having committed such evil deeds, how can there again be liberation?
Explain that, O Blessed One; I wish to hear it in truth." / The Blessed Lord said: / "Having engaged in intercourse with them, [embracing] a red-hot iron doll,
Embracing [it], he should yield his life-breath; purified, he would go to another world. / That man indeed who, having abandoned the household order, becomes fixed in mind on me,
[And] constantly remembers Govinda, achieves the destruction of all sins. / [Even if] ten thousand murders of a Brahmin were committed by him, or the violation of a guru's wife,
A hundred or a hundred thousand [sins] from drinking flour-liquor, / Committing theft of gold and the like, or prolonged association with them—
These and other sins, as well as the great mortal crimes, / Just as cotton or dry grass is destroyed upon reaching fire, perish entirely.
Therefore, having remembered my name, Govinda, a man becomes purified. / Or he who remains in the household order, constantly making the proclamation of Govinda,
And having worshipped, is ferried across sin. / On the delightful bank of the Bhāgīrathī, during an auspicious eclipse of the sun,
Whatever fruit a man obtains by giving ten million cows, / That fruit he fully attains, and a thousand times more,
By chanting Govinda's name, dear one, and he dwells imperishably in my city. / Dwelling at will in my abode, he becomes a sovereign king.
Hearing the stories about me in a Purāṇa, a man attains resemblance to me. / And having narrated a Purāṇa, he attains union with Viṣṇu.
Therefore, a Purāṇa, which is a collection of dharma, should be heard constantly; / It should be recited with effort; he goes to the form of Viṣṇu in that world.
Or whatever other fault is committed with regard to women, it will surely be mitigated as appropriate. / Listen, I will declare it to you in truth, O delight of the twice-born!
By the gift of all kinds of seeds together with a water jar, a great fruit [is won]; / One should give it to a Brahmin on an auspicious day; he immediately becomes purified in an instant.
One should give all seeds such as grains to a twice-born man at the proper time; / Having brought about the destruction of all sins, he enjoys imperishable heaven.
I will speak of the firm virtue of chaste wives, O Brahmin-sage! / Her lineage becomes pure, and fortune constantly attends [her].
There is heaven for both lineages: that of her husband and her own. / The virtue of a devoted wife, O Brahmin, was forgotten as you asked;
I shall speak again for women, an auspicious benefit for all the world. / Having dwelt [thus] in former times, women through merit and demerit,
And thereafter devoted to their husbands, they go to my abode. / For six months or for a year—and more is praised—
She who becomes a devoted wife, as long as she is purified, goes to heaven. / Even a husband who drinks liquor, slays a Brahmin, or is laden with all sins,
She who follows her husband leads him, purified from the mire, to heaven. / A husband like the god of love, and she charming like Ratī,
Enjoys endless pleasure for a long time in the world of Indra. / And she who, by the power of devotion to her husband, when her lord falls afar,
Having obtained a token [of his] and died in the fire, delivers her husband from sin. / And a devoted woman whose husband dies in another land,
She, taking her husband's token and sleeping in the fire, goes to heaven. / But a woman of the Brahmin class who follows her dead husband—
She, by killing herself, does not lead herself nor her husband to heaven. / A Brahmin woman must not die going along [with him], by the ordinance of Brahmā;
She who kills herself attains the fate of an ascetic [who falls from vows] upon dying. / The best of men said: / The Brahmin is declared praiseworthy among all castes,
And [what is done] by the foremost of the twice-born is meritorious; why then is there a reverse here? / The Blessed Lord said: / A rash deed is never proper for a Brahmin woman;
By completely killing her, that man would become a slayer of a Brahmin. / Therefore, a woman of the Brahmin caste, being twice-born, should observe an ascetic vow.
I will declare it as it is; listen truly, O Brahmin! / She should never eat meat from the marketplace.
In one year she obtains the fruit of a thousand horse sacrifices. / Worship of one's chosen deity, Hari, is an unequalled observance;
She should offer water and rice balls for her master without envy. / For thousands of crores of cosmic ages, and hundreds of crores of cosmic ages,
That virtuous woman remains joined with her husband in the world of Viṣṇu. / Then, having undertaken that great vow, a Brahmin wife in hell
Would deliver both lineages by the hundreds and by the thousands. / Therefore, the relatives themselves—sons, brothers, and the like, who are wise—
Restraining her, should never cause the breach of her vow. / If, on reaching the day of Hari, a widow does not observe the vow,
That unfortunate woman attains widowhood again in birth after birth. / From the eating of fish and meat, and from the abandonment of vows,
Having gone to hell for a long time, she surely becomes a female dog. / The wicked widow, a destroyer of her family, who engages in sexual intercourse,
Having experienced hells, then becomes a female vulture for ten births, / Becomes a female jackal for two births, and then attains human status.
Likewise, from child-widowhood she falls into servitude. / The twice-born said: / Speak of the fruit of giving a daughter in marriage; tell also what the fruit of giving a female slave is,
And the ritual procedure as prescribed, if you have favor toward me, O Lord! / The Blessed Lord said: / To one endowed with beauty, full of good qualities, of noble birth, youthful,
Prosperous, and filled with wealth—hear the fruit of giving a daughter [to such a groom]: / He who gives a virgin endowed with all ornaments,
By him the entire earth with its mountains, forests, and groves is given. / By the gift of [a maiden with] half the ornaments, the fruit surely accrues to the giver;
For a maiden without ornaments, there is a fourth of the fruit. / But the man who takes a bride-price goes to hell;
Having sold his own daughter, the fool does not turn back from hell. / He who out of greed gives his daughter to an unsuitable man,
Attaining the Raurava hell, goes to the state of a Cāṇḍāla. / For this very reason, a wise man never takes a bride-price from a son-in-law
Even in his mind; what is given to him becomes imperishable. / Land, a cow, gold, wealth, clothing, and grain—
Having given [these] as a dowry to the son-in-law, all becomes imperishable. / At the time of marriage, my child, by people of the same gotra or of another gotra,
Whatever dowry is given, all that becomes imperishable. / If the giver does not remember the gift, and the recipient does not ask for it,
The two of them go to hell, like a jar whose rope is severed. / A dowry gift must certainly be given by a virtuous person;
Not having given it, he reaches hell and incurs servitude. / To one who is too close, too far away, exceedingly rich, exceedingly destitute,
Lacking noble birth, and foolish—to these six a daughter is not given. / To one who is exceedingly old, exceedingly pitiable, sickly, [merely] residing in the country,
Exceedingly angry, or discontented—to these six a daughter is not given. / Having given a virgin to these, one goes to hell,
Out of greed, desire for honor, or an exchange of maidens. / A woman dear to sages, youthful and endowed with beauty,
Having given [her] with ornaments and a bed, he obtains endless fruit. / And the fruit of these two, a young woman and a maiden, for you:
One should be given to a bridegroom, but the other to a Brahmin. / A purchased woman should be given to a deity by a steadfast man of untroubled action;
His stay in heaven will last for an eon, or he will be a king possessing great wealth on earth. / In each birth he obtains an excellent wife of radiant complexion.
He who constantly listens to this unequalled sacred narrative, / His sins are all destroyed, and he masters the meaning of all scriptures;
He attains imperishable heaven, becomes beloved to women, / Or, as a kṣatriya, he will surely become victorious and a lord of the world.
the heard [account] takes away the sins committed in birth after birth; / and likewise a noble woman obtains good fortune in the world."

1.53.m: The twice-born said: / "You ought to speak in full, O lord, of the deeds and peerless majesty of Tulādhāra, / if you have favor toward me."
The Blessed Lord said: / "Whoever gives out of a truthful nature, from lack of greed, and from absence of malice, / for him a hundred sacrifices are perpetually completed with good sacrificial gifts.
By truth the sun rises, and likewise the wind blows; / the ocean does not transgress its shore, nor the tortoise [transgress] the earth.
By truth all the worlds endure, and all the mountains; / and that being who has fallen from truth certainly becomes a dweller of the lower regions.
He who is devoted to truthful speech and always devoted to truthful action, / having reached heaven with his physical body, attains imperishability.
By truth all the sages have reached me and attained stability; / by truth King Yudhiṣṭhira went to heaven with his physical body.
Having conquered the entire host of enemies, the world was protected by him through dharma; / and he performed the pure, very rare Rājasūya sacrifice.
And eighty-four thousand brahmins / he would feed daily from golden vessels and with royal utensils.
Having fed them, he would dismiss them after giving them the utensils; / and whatever wealth was desired by the twice-born, he would have given to them beyond that.

Then, knowing the assembly of the twice-born to be free from poverty, he would let them depart; / likewise, sixteen thousand snātakas / the king, free from malice, would feed daily solely through truth.
Formerly they stayed long in his house out of a desire for victory; / by him the whole world was conquered on account of bestowing grace on living beings.
And through truth the asura King Bali will become Indra; / for him who dwells in Pātāla, I constantly abide in his dwelling.
And I dwell perpetually in the heart of him whose deeds are solely meritorious; / or, as formerly he was bound by me, because of his release from the demon womb,
I grant the nether world, immortality, and the status of Indra. / King Hariścandra, through truth, along with his vehicles and retinue,
is established in Satyaloka with his own pure body. / Many other kings and those who are perfected great sages,
wise men, and ascetics, all became imperishable through truth; / therefore, one devoted to truth in the world is capable of deliverance from cyclic existence.
The great-souled Tulādhāra is indeed firmly established in truthful speech; / there is none equal to him in the world on account of his truthful speech.
Truth was weighed on a balance against a thousand horse sacrifices; / indeed, truth alone outweighs a thousand horse sacrifices.
Everything can be achieved through truth; truth is indeed insurmountable; / through truthful speech, that cow Bahulā went to heaven.
Having pacified the whole kingdom, return [to worldly existence] is rare; / likewise, this witness is always [truthful]; he is never untruthful.
A wise man, in buying and selling, whether high-priced or low-priced, / should have truthful speech that is praised, especially in the case of a witness.
Witnesses, having spoken the truth, have gone to imperishable heaven; / an eloquent master of speech, having entered an assembly, speaks the truth;
he goes to Brahmā's abode, which is difficult to attain even through other sacrifices. / Whoever speaks the truth in an assembly obtains the fruit of a horse sacrifice.
Speaking falsely out of greed or hatred, one goes to the Raurava hell. / Tulādhāra is the witness of all, and indeed a hero among men.
Particularly by renouncing greed, one attains immortality in heaven. / There was a certain noble Śūdra who was never given to greed.
His livelihood was made with difficulty by vegetables and by gleaning ears of grain; / his pair of garments was worn out, and his hands were always his eating vessel.
Though always lacking gain, he never took another's property. / To test him, I took a pair of garments,
and, remaining on the riverbank under a cover, placed it respectfully. / Seeing that pair of garments, he did not set his mind on greed.
Knowing it belonged to someone else, he went to his own house with patience. / Then, O twice-born, reflecting in my heart: 'This is too little,'
I dropped an udumbara fruit containing gold right there, / on the riverbank, in an isolated, deserted bend.
When he went to that place, that wonder was seen by him: / 'Enough! This seems to be an artificial arrangement.
If I take it now, my freedom from greed is utterly lost. / Guarding it is misery, and it is a cause of egotism.
Where there is greed, there is [desire for] gain; from gain, greed proceeds. / And for a man seized by greed, there is eternal hell.
If flawed wealth stays in the house, / then madness indeed arises in my wife and sons.
From madness comes delusion of mind through distortions born of lust; / from delusion comes confusion, then egotism, and after that anger and greed.
And through their abundance, asceticism will go to destruction. / When asceticism is destroyed, the mind-deluding impurities persist,
and bound by those chain-like attachments, one can never attain deliverance.' / Considering this, that Śūdra left it and went home.
Standing in heaven, the gods joyfully said there: 'Well done! Well done!' / Then, assuming the form of a Jain ascetic, near his house
I went and spoke of divine counsel, narrating what had occurred. / Then, through repeated contact and the gathering of people,
his wife came and asked about the divine matter. / Then I told her what was in her heart at once;
secretly the cause of the sound of fortune was told by me: / 'What was intended for you, given by destiny, was abandoned by your husband like a fool.
It was cast away, O fortunate lady! There is no more wealth for you here. / As long as he lives, he will undoubtedly experience misfortune.
Go home, mother, to the empty house; ask him about what was not obtained.' / Hearing that speech, she went to her husband's presence,
and spoke of his bad conduct. Hearing that, he was astonished. / Reflecting, he came with her into my presence.
Secretly he said to me: 'Tell me of your ascetic state.' / The ascetic said: 'How could something visible, long purified, be cast aside by you like grass, in sport?
Because, dear friend, there is no unhindered fortune [greater than that] which you abandoned! / Incomparable sovereignty, heroism, and prosperity crumble away.
You will continually see with your own eyes the great suffering of your kin, / from birth until death, which is the certain fate of those who die.
Therefore, let it be taken quickly! Enjoy unhindered pleasure, / incomparable sovereignty, heroism, and the supreme wonder of the worlds.'
The Śūdra said: 'I have no desire for wealth. Wealth is the snare of saṃsāra; / a mortal fallen into its grasp does not attain liberation again.
Hear the fault of wealth in this world and in the next: / fear of thieves, of kinsmen, and of kings and their taxes.
All mortals are murderous, like animals, fish, and birds of prey. / Likewise, for the wealthy, how can worldly goods bring happiness?
Wealth is the destroyer of life and the accomplisher of wicked deeds; / it is the dear home of death and others, the supreme cause of misfortune.'
The ascetic said: 'He who has wealth has friends; he who has wealth has kinsmen; / [wealth brings] lineage, good character, learning, beauty, enjoyment, fame, and happiness.
For one devoid of wealth, however, and abandoned by sons and wife, / how can there be a friend? How dharma? What kind of birth is it for the wretched?
The performance of sacrifices such as sattva and others, the beneficial digging of ponds, / and giving gifts, which is the stairway to heaven—none of these is accomplished for a man of no means.
Observing the performance of vows, the constant hearing of dharma and such, / rites for the ancestors and pilgrimages—none is accomplished for one without wealth.
Likewise, the remedy for disease, proper diet, the accumulation of medicine, / protection, war, and certainly the conquest of enemies [require wealth].
And the livelihood of women from birth is obtained through the union with wealth. / Whatever good deeds and bad deeds are performed by the past and the future—
therefore, he who has abundant wealth can enjoy at will. / You will attain heaven very soon from charity alone.'

The Śūdra said: 'Through desirelessness is all observance; through freedom from anger is resort to holy places; / through compassion and recitation of prayers is one equal and pure; contentment alone is wealth.
Non-violence is the supreme perfection; the life of gleaning ears of grain is best; / an intake of vegetables is equal to nectar; fasting is supreme austerity.
Contentment is my great enjoyment; a cowrie shell is my great gift; / another's wife is like a mother, and another's goods are like a clod of earth.
Another's wife is like a serpent. This is my entire sacrifice. / Therefore I will not take it; truly, truly, O mine of virtues!
Better than washing off mud is not touching it from afar.' / When this was said, O best of men, a shower of flowers fell,
O twice-born, upon the crown of his head and his body, released by all the gods. / The drums of the gods resounded, and the hosts of apsarases danced.
The lords of the gandharvas sang, and an aerial chariot descended from the sky. / The hosts of gods said there: 'Mount this aerial chariot!
Reaching Satyaloka, enjoy pleasures like great Indra! / Even if calculated, your period of enjoyment will endure, O righteous one!'
And when the gods had spoken thus, the śūdra said these words: / 'How can there be knowledge, gesture, and speech in this Nirgrantha?'
Is he Hari and Hara, or Brahmā? Or is he Indra or Bṛhaspati? / Or has Dharma himself come here in person to test me?'
When this was said, that mendicant smiled and spoke these words: / 'In order to know your dharma, I, Viṣṇu, have come here.'
Go to heaven in the aerial chariot with your family, O great sage! / By my favor, you all shall possess eternal youth;
it shall be so, O very wise one! You will obtain boundless fortune.' / Endowed with divine ornaments and adorned with divine garments,
they immediately went to heaven, accompanied by all their kinsmen. / Thus, O best of twice-born, through the renunciation of greed they went to heaven.
Likewise, the wise Tulādhāra is established in truthful dharma, / by which he knows that event which occurred in another land.
There is no one equal to Tulādhāra established in the realm of the gods. / Therefore, you too, O earthly god, become equal to him and go to heaven.
The mortal who hears this, being established in all dharma, / has the sin accumulated over many births destroyed in that very instant.
By merely reading it once, one obtains the fruit of all sacrifices. / He shall become venerable among gods and before men, O vipra.

1.54.m: The Blessed Lord said: / The greatness of Adrohaka, unbearable to the world, has been told; / having forgiven a beautiful woman who shared his bed, he became all-conquering.
Hard to master even for the wise, for sages, and for celibate students, / an uneven path for gods, asuras, and humans—he traversed it smoothly.
What man is capable of conquering passion, which is perverse by nature? / Except for Adrohaka, O twice-born, that man alone conquered worldly existence.
From the abduction of Ahalyā alone did the lord of the gods become marked with vulvas; / and by the grace of the goddess he became renowned as the Thousand-Eyed.
It is known in the entire world, in the three worlds with the moving and unmoving. / The twice-born said: And how did the abduction of Ahalyā by the god of gods happen, O Lord?
And how did the lord of the gods, the Thousand-Eyed, become marked with vulvas? / How did the king of the gods, though not marked with signs, become marked with vulvas?
Ill is the hearing of the disfigurement of a god; I wish to hear it accurately. / The Blessed Lord said: Formerly, the lord of the world, the high-minded Creator,
gladly gave to Gautama a maiden born of his own mind, in the presence of the guardians of the world. / Then, of the guardians of the world whose minds were possessed by love,
and of the husband of Śacī, a delusion remained in their hearts like an arrow: / 'Bypassing the guardians of the world, this fair-complexioned woman, beautifully adorned,
who is like a gem, was given to a twice-born! What am I to do?' / Thus deliberating, while her youth was unfolding,
her exceedingly radiant form was again seen by him through illusion. / Still thinking of her, he went to the dwelling of Gautama.
Hear from me what happened after he went there: / Once, Gautama went to Puṣkara to bathe.
And the virtuous woman was occupied with cleansing the house and household belongings, / engaged in offering oblations for the dwelling of the deities,
gathering firewood, performing fire-rites, and attending to daily duties. / In the meantime, Śakra assumed the form and body
of that great sage and gladly entered the hut. / Seeing her husband, the faithful and devoted wife,
with supreme faith, prepared to arrange the articles in the place of the gods. / Then Hari, wearing the garb of the sage, afflicted [with passion], said to her:
'Subdued by Pradyumna, O lovely one, give me a kiss and the rest.' / In the meantime, she, filled with bashfulness, spoke these words:
'You ought not to speak to me, O lord, setting aside rites for the gods and the like. / You know everything, O knower of dharma, the certainty of merits, O sage.
Indeed, this matter is not suitable at this very hour.' / Then, seeing her who was lovely in every limb, afflicted by passion,
[he said:] 'Enough, beloved, do not speak so; love is born within my heart! / What ought to be done and what ought not to be done is determined by the husband's word.
She who always does so is a devoted wife. / But she who transgresses his command, especially in sexual intercourse,
her merit is destroyed and she meets a wretched fate.' / She said: 'The divine articles are meant for the gods, O sage;
and the other daily rites—how can there be any disruption of them?' / He said to the chaste woman: 'Give me your embrace and the rest;
abandoning fear in your mind, they have been granted by me.' / Having spoken thus and embraced her, his desire was accomplished by him.
In the meantime, O twice-born, a blemish appeared in the sage's heart; / then, entering into meditation, he discovered the deed of the husband of Śacī.
He quickly went and stood at the entrance of the doorway. / Śakra, however, noticing the sage, entered the body of a cat.
He ran along the path of the fleeing cat; / the sage spoke to him there: 'Who are you, assuming the form of a cat?'
Out of fear, Śakra stood before that sage with folded hands. / Seeing Maghavan before him, the preeminent sage was enraged:
'Since such a deed of reckless deceit was done by you for the sake of the vulva, / therefore let a thousand splendid vulvas be upon your limbs!
May it be so here, O most wicked one; and your penis shall fall off! / Depart from my presence, fool! The denizens of heaven in the realm of the gods,
the foremost sages, men, and Siddhas, along with serpents, will look upon you!' / Having spoken thus, the best of sages asked that devoted wife, who was weeping:
'What terrible deed has now befallen you?' / Addressed thus, trembling and afraid, she spoke to her husband:
'You ought to forgive whatever deed was done out of ignorance, O lord.' / The sage said: 'You were approached by another, impure and evil-doing as you are!
Reduced to skin and bone, without flesh, devoid of nails, / you will remain for a long time, alone, and people and women will look upon you!'
Afflicted, she said to him: 'Let an end to the curse be ordained.' / When this was said, filled with compassion, though also flooded with anger,
Gautama spoke these words: 'When Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, / Viṣṇu, comes to the forest accompanied by Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa,
having seen you afflicted, withered, bodiless, standing on the path, / Rāma will indeed say, laughing before Vasiṣṭha:
"What is this withered figure, an effigy made of bones, a corpse? / Such a form, inverted from the world, has never been seen by me before, O Brahmin."
Then Vasiṣṭha will recount to the fortunate Rāma, / Viṣṇu in human form, what had happened formerly.
Having heard Vasiṣṭha's words, Rāma, who knows dharma, will say: / "There is no fault in her at all; this fault lies with the chastiser of Pāka."
When spoken to thus by Rāma, having cast off that repulsive form / and assumed a divine form, you will come to my house.'
Having cursed her, Gautama indeed went to the forest to perform austerities; / then, utterly withered in form, she remained standing in that very manner on the path.
Only by the word of Rāma did she return to Gautama. / Gautama too, along with her, remains today thus in heaven.
Indra too, filled with shame, stayed within the waters for a long time. / And having stayed within the waters, he praised the goddess named Indrākṣī.
Then the goddess, highly pleased and satisfied by that hymn of praise, / approached and said: 'Let a boon be chosen from me!'
Then Śakra, conqueror of enemies' cities, spoke this to the goddess: / 'By your favor, O goddess, having cast off my deformity born of the sage's curse,
and having regained sovereignty over the gods, may I be as before.' / Then the goddess said to him: 'That evil born of the sage's curse,
even gods such as Brahmā are not able to destroy, O lord of the gods! / But I shall today devise an idea by which it will not be noticed by the worlds:
A thousand eyes will appear within the vulvas; / known as the Thousand-Eyed, you will rule over the gods.
And by my boon, a ram's testicle will become your penis.' / Having spoken thus, that Mother of the Universe disappeared right there.
Śakra, worthy of worship by the foremost gods, lives in heaven even today. / Such was the condition of Indra due to passion, O best of the twice-born.

1.55.m: The Blessed Lord said: And I shall speak of another who was dominated by passion: / Formerly, on the bank of the Bhāgīrathī, there was a twice-born, a Paramahaṃsa,
a teacher of thousands of twice-born, a supreme giver of peace, / bearing a single staff, staying on the earth like a tortoise.
While he was alone in that cleaned temple, / a woman set out at evening from her husband's house to go to another.
Suddenly he encountered a young woman endowed with beauty; / seeing her, the venerable brāhmaṇa was afflicted with fear of the god of desire.
He put her into the interior of the house and spent the night [there]; / making the bolt secure in the very beautiful temple,
she never allowed him to enter through the door at all. / Being in such a state, though situated in deep meditation, having passed the night and weeping,
thinking of that beautiful woman, [he wondered], "What has happened at my door?" / Reflecting thus, he said to her, "Grant entry to us here, beloved!
And your husband will become submissive, lovely woman, and dear to you." / Then she spoke to that old brāhmaṇa who was deeply yearning through lust:
"Father, you ought not to utter such improper words, lord!" / Then that venerable one said, "I have abundant wealth;
I will give it to you, auspicious lady; open the door-leaf!" / And she said again to the brāhmaṇa, "Indeed, by dharma you are my father.
Do not approach me, a daughter and another's wife, O righteous one!" / Reflecting in his mind, [attempting to enter] the house by a narrow opening,
and pushing open [a space] with his arm, he endeavored to enter. / And as he was going, half the door-leaf [caught] his head in a tight trap;
having entered, it could not come back out, and he then died. / At dawn, the watchmen and attendants who arrived
saw that astonishing corpse, and astonished, they said to her: / "How did his death come to pass? Tell us, fair one!"
Having related the whole incident, she went to her desired place. / Thus the power of desire is uncontrollable among people,
and affects all living beings—gods, asuras, and humans. / Seeing the beautiful Amoghā, the grandfather of all the worlds
shed his seed there; from that, Lauhitya is traditionally said to have been born. / He purifies all the worlds, for he consists of all holy places.
Resorting to him, a person goes to the painless world of Brahmā." / The brāhmaṇa said: "How did Brahmā's delusion come about? And who was this lovely woman, Amoghā?
I wish to hear the origin of that king of holy places in truth." / The blessed Lord said: "There was a sage worshipful even to the gods, equal in radiance to Brahmā,
renowned as Śantanu, whose devoted wife / was known as Amoghā, endowed with beauty and youth.
To look for her husband, Brahmā went to their house. / At that time the best of sages had gone to the forest for flowers and the like.
Seeing that best of the gods, she offered the water offering, foot-washing water, and the rest; / bowing from afar, she entered the house.
Seeing her of faultless limbs, the Creator fell under the power of desire. / Collecting himself, the Creator thought of her as she stood before him.
The seed of the supreme spirit Brahmā fell upon the couch. / Thereupon Brahmā departed, afraid and tormented with haste.
Then the sage returned home and saw semen on the seat. / He asked that beautiful woman, "Has any man come here?"
Then Amoghā said to him: "Brahmā came here indeed, husband, / only in search of you, lord. The seat here was offered by me.
You ought to discover through ascetic power the cause of the semen here." / Then through meditation that was recognized by that very twice-born.
"Chaste woman, protect the supreme semen of Brahmā by my command. / A son shall be born to you, the sole purifier of all worlds;
all our heart's desire for what is auspicious will bear fruit." / Then, faithful to her husband, having accepted his command, for the sake of the conception,
that fortunate lady drank the semen of the supreme spirit Brahmā. / A swirling vortex arose, throbbing as a fierce embryo.
She was not able to endure it, and she then said to Śantanu: / "I cannot bear the fetus now, my lord, O master!
What shall I do, knower of dharma? Even my life-breath is trembling. / Instruct me, highly fortunate one, where I may release the fetus."
Receiving her husband's command, the fetus was released at Yugandhara / as pure water full of radiance, grounded in all dharma.
In its midst was a pure man wearing a diadem and blue clothes, / his limbs encircled with a string of jewels, hard to behold like a multitude of lights.
Then the hosts of gods showered a rain of flowers from heaven. / Manifested among all holy places, he is remembered as the king of holy places.
[Rāma said:] "Then I was born in the lineage of Bhṛgu, renowned as Rāma. / Having slain the kṣatriyas who were the killers of my father, together with their armies, forces, and vehicles,
when they went to battle and were terrified, I was covered with all kinds of mire; / a terrible state resembling the killing of a brāhmaṇa stood upon my household.
My mire-covered axe, though washed, would not become clean at all. / Then a voice arose in the sky: 'Rāma, follow my word!
In whatever holy place your axe becomes spotless here, / there the destruction of all sins committed by you shall come to pass.
Stay there for the welfare of all people, O giver of honor! / Go swiftly to all the holy places, even the very great ones.
If among them your axe becomes clean in a great holy place, / know that one among holy places to be proclaimed as conferring liberation.'"
Hearing that, the son of Jamadagni then set out for the holy places: / to the Gaṅgā, the bright Sarasvatī, the Kāverī, and the Sarayū,
to the Godāvarī, the Yamunā, the Kadrū, and the Vasudā, / and to the other charming, auspicious Gaurī situated in the east, which bestows merit.
As that steadfast one, swift as the wind, went on, / [the axe] washed at all the holy places still did not become spotless.
Then that Hari went to an inaccessible mountain cave, a great forest, a mountain, / an inaccessible mountain peak, and to a holy place.
Still his axe did not attain spotlessness by that means; / there Rāma, conqueror of enemies' cities, fell into despair.
Saying "Alas! Alas!" in various ways and sitting down on the surface of the earth, / the hero fell into deep sorrow. Again [a voice] spoke to him thus:
"In the eastern direction, lord of gods, there is a holy place within the cavity of a cave." / Hearing that, that tiger among men went and saw a pool,
with a whirlpool moving clockwise, bright, sin-removing, and auspicious. / By the mere touch of its water, the axe attained purity.
Then Rāma, filled with joy, performed an ablution; / of him whose soul was purified and free from sin, a mind bringing great purification arose.
Having stayed there for a very long time and propitiated that king of holy places, / that Rāma, endowed with speed, went from that mountain to the city.
Having made it renowned on earth, he then went to the salt ocean. / This excellent holy place was made directly on earth by the Grandfather;
it confers happiness, is entirely pure, and indeed grants the path to liberation. / Thus know the power of desire to be irresistible and unbearable.
From desire, virtue and sin arise, and merit through the application of merit. / And thus Lauhitya was born as the legitimate son of Virañci,
born in the field of Śantanu and produced from the womb of Amoghā. / Desire was conquered by Viriñci, and by Śantanu through absence of malice,
and by her wifely devotion; therefore he is the best of holy places. / Thus, whoever recites this meritorious, auspicious narrative daily,
or listens to it with joy on earth, goes upon the path to liberation.

1.56.m: The Blessed Lord said: / Formerly Śarva, seeing young, shapely women from all quarters, / belonging to Gandharvas, Kinnaras, and humans,
attracted them by a mantra far away into the sky. / Under the pretext of penance, the god, his mind fixated on them,
made a most delightful hut, and with them Maheśvara / suddenly engaged in sport, overcome by the god of love.
Meanwhile, the mind of Gaurī became agitated; / through the yoga of meditation, she saw the Lord of the Universe sporting.
Knowing that he had entered into intimacy with women, she came under the sway of wrath; / then, assuming the form of Kṣemaṅkarī, she entered [there].
In a secluded spot of the sky, far away, [she saw] the radiant Puruṣa, the Supreme Puruṣa, / shining like the god of love, seated amidst beautiful women,
embracing and sporting repeatedly with the women, / kissing [them] deeply—the god Hara tormented by passion.
Seeing what had occurred, Kṣemaṅkarī then descended before [him]; / pulling them by the hair, she struck them with her feet.
Afflicted by shame, Śarva remained turning away his face. / Pulling them by the hair in rage, she threw them down to the surface of the earth.
All the women, upon reaching the earth, instantly had disfigured faces; / their limbs scorched by Umā's curse, they fell into the power of Mlecchas.
They became known as Cāṇḍāla women, with or without husbands; / even today, all of them suffer the curse laid by Umā.
Then Umā, having assumed a hundred forms, united with the Lord. / Know thus, O twice-born, the constant power of desire.
Then, after a long time, he went with her to his abode on Kailāsa. / Therefore, the mortals who revere Kṣemaṅkarī upon seeing her,
their wealth, prosperity, and majesty increase here and in the hereafter. / 'O you whose whole body is red with saffron, whose face is white as jasmine and the moon,
bestower of all auspiciousness, O Goddess Kṣemaṅkarī, praise be to you!' / Even by equality with the Yoginī, whether turned toward her or turned away,
he who does not bow down upon seeing her suffers defeat in battle; / by bowing down, victory shall be obtained in royal houses and in learning.
Such is the power of desire; Bhava came under the sway of delusion. / Yet this [man] attained mastery over gods and Asuras by forbearance.
None equal to him has ever existed or will ever exist in the world; / having abandoned a lovely woman seated on his lap and lying on the bed of patience,
he won worlds that are very hard for gods and Asuras to attain. / Thus, as foremost among the Vaiṣṇavas, he is worshipped by the hosts of gods and Asuras,
who does not offer the best of food [to another] and eats the remainder himself. / When a long time had passed pleasantly through such fortitude of practice,
seeing his wife before union, he gladly gave me [first place]; / resolving upon twelve years, the enjoyment was first directed toward me.
Because of that, I dwell constantly in his house for its protection; / likewise, he always yearns for the pure essence of the myrobalan fruit.
Therefore, among all other Vaiṣṇavas, he is spoken of by me as the [true] Vaiṣṇava. / O brahmin, the devotees and gods who walked my path in the past,
what was not done even by them has been pre-eminently done by him. / Therefore, the charming name 'Vaiṣṇavasarvasva' was given [to him] by me.
I dwell in his home and do not depart even for a moment. / Therefore, to those who are my devotees in this way, I am easily attained, O twice-born.
I give our own state to them today for my own purpose. / O brahmin, our kindness, dreams, food, and the rest are equal;
behold, O earth-god, absorption and companionship, with no difference between us! / Then Mūka and all the others, having welcomed Hari, the Lord,
the righteous ones wishing to go to heaven, with their wives and attendants, / and even the house lizards that were near their house,
and the various worms and insects that were there, followed them, O gods! / Vyāsa said: Meanwhile, the gods, Siddhas, and supreme ṛṣis
sent down rains of flowers, shouting 'Well done! Well done!' / Divine drums sounded in the celestial chariots and in the groves.
Mounting each their own chariot, they went to the city along Hari's path. / Seeing that marvel, the brahmin spoke to Janārdana:
"O Lord of the gods, O Madhusūdana, tell me the instruction!" / The Blessed Lord said: "Go to your parents, my child, whose minds are agitated with grief.
Having served them with effort, you shall reach my abode before long. / Deities equal to a father and mother do not exist in the realm of the gods.
By them this much-despised body was constantly protected in infancy; / accompanied by the defect of ignorance, it was nourished and caused to grow.
There is nothing equal to those two in the three worlds, both moving and unmoving." / Then all the hosts of gods, filled with joy along with those five,
praising Mādhava, went to Hari's abode— / a delightful city inlaid [with gems], fashioned by Viśvakarman,
rich in gems, filled with desires, accompanied by wish-fulfilling trees and the like, / variegated with all kinds of jewels, with dwellings made of gold,
with stairways of diamond and lapis lazuli, joined with the waters of the heavenly river, / filled with singing and instrumental music, furnished with all kinds of fortresses,
abounding in the calls of cuckoos, attended by Siddhas and Gandharvas, / filled with good people endowed with beauty, a city as though traveling in the sky.
Then, remaining there, all of them [later] fell from above all the worlds. / The twice-born too, having gone to his parents and served them with effort,
went to Hari with his family in no long time. / This sacred Pañcākhyāna has thus been proclaimed to you by me;
whoever reads or hears it has no misfortune in this world; / he is never tainted by sins such as the killing of a brahmin.
Whatever fruit a man obtains by the gift of ten million cows, / that fruit he fully obtains by immersing himself in the Pañcākhyāna.
Whatever fruit is attained by bathing daily at Puṣkara and constantly in the Bhāgīrathī, / that he attains from the reach of hearing [it] but once.
It swiftly destroys bad dreams and bestows health; / it brings fortune and health; therefore it should indeed be heard.

1.57.m: The twice-born said: / Fame and dharma, which are considered foremost among all in the worlds— / tell us [of them], O tiger among sages, if you have favor toward us.
Vyāsa said: / In whose excavated reservoir cows are satisfied even for a month in the forest, / or from seven days, he is purified and worshipped by all the gods.
Especially by a pond purified through the rite of sacrifice— / whatever fruit comes from the giving of water, hear all that here:
Year after year, and kalpa after kalpa, it is ordained; / through giving, the giver of water, giving everything on earth, attains heaven.
As many drops as are produced when a cloud rains upon the excavation, / for so many thousands of years does a mortal enjoy heaven.
Through water and through the cooking of food and the like, a man becomes gratified; / and without food, the maintenance of the life-breaths cannot occur.
The libation to the ancestors, purification, form, and the destruction of bad odors, / indeed all the seed gathered here—everything is established in water.
The washing of clothes, as well as the cleaning of vessels, is pleasing; / with it alone every task is done, and drinking water is indeed pure.
Therefore, with every effort, with all one's strength, / and likewise with all one's wealth, one should have a step-well, a well, or a pond constructed.
Whoever provides a reservoir of water in a waterless region, / for him a kalpa in heaven is decreed for each day [it provides water].
Falling from heaven, he becomes a brāhmaṇa who has mastered the meaning of the Vedas and śāstras, / a friend of all beings and righteous-minded; after performing austerities, he goes to heaven.
Having obtained eight such births, his [merit] is considered imperishable; / born into a family of kṣatriyas, he becomes a sovereign king.
A vaiśya gains imperishable wealth that is pleasing birth after birth; / and śūdras and other outcasts repeatedly attain heaven.
A man who digs a well four cubits in measure, / constantly beneficent to others, spends a kalpa in heaven for every year [it lasts].
For double [the size], one should know it is double [the reward], and for fourfold, a hundredfold; / but whoever provides a lotus pool twenty cubits in measure,
even he attains the abode of Viṣṇu and likewise divine enjoyment; / afterwards, having been born a king, he becomes wealthy and an eloquent speaker.
Thus twofold, threefold, or even fourfold enjoyment is expected according to quality; / know that if it is spacious, the reward is abundant; through a thousand cubits, one does not fall from heaven.
By double a thousand, a man becomes honored by the gods; / as many living beings as there are who sustained their life there,
that number of people become his servants, clinging to his back, / constantly in his house, in the city, and in the countrysides.
Just as birds go to the forest when its fruit is depleted, leaving behind their protector, / so a bird, a boar, a buffalo cow, and a female elephant,
the adviser, and the builder—these six go to heaven. / For birds, one should declare a hundred divine years in heaven;
for a boar, a thousand years, but for a buffalo cow, ten thousand years; / assuming a divine form, for a female elephant a hundred thousand [years] is proclaimed;
ten million for the adviser, and for the builder [the reward] is truly imperishable. / Formerly, a reservoir was made by a son of a wealthy man, renowned,
with an expenditure of ten thousand pieces of wealth, with his own vital breath and strength, / for the welfare of all living beings, endowed with faith in Śiva.
After some time, he became depleted of wealth; / a certain wealthy man desiring it stepped forward to pay its price.
Having reflected, the wealthy man spoke—listen now to his words: / 'I shall give you ten thousand dīnāras for the sake of this [pool].
You consider the merit obtained from the lotus pool as gain;' / having offered the price according to his ability, he resolved to make it his own.
When this was said, he said to him: 'The daily fruit of merit is indeed / ten thousandfold, as those who know merit understand.
In this waterless land, an auspicious excavation was made by me; / all people perform bathing, drinking, and other acts according to their wish.
Therefore, a daily reward of ten thousand [coins] is expected for me.' / Then he and the members of the assembly laughed at him.
Afflicted with shame, he uttered these words: / 'This word of mine is true; make a test according to dharma.'
Out of spite, that [wealthy man] said to him: 'Listen to my word, father: / giving you this ten thousand dīnāras, and bringing a stone,
I will throw it into your excavation; let it sink suitably. / At what time the stone emerges and floats across,
my wealth will not go to ruin; otherwise, it is indeed mine by dharma.' / Saying 'Very well,' he took the ten thousand and went to his own home.
In the presence of witnesses, the stone was thrown by him / into that great lotus pool, and it was witnessed by mortals, gods, and asuras.
Then, on the scale of dharma, it was weighed by the witness of dharma: / the gift of ten thousand dīnāras, and the water of the lotus pool.
Even a single day of water was not equal [to it], greatly exceeding it by dharma; / there was mental grief for the wealthy man, and on the next day his wealth was futile.
A pile of stones emerged, floating upon the water like an island. / Then a tumultuous shouting of the people arose.
Hearing that wonderful report, the two came there with joy; / seeing the stony pile become like that, he made ten thousand [offerings] likewise.
Then by the owner of the excavation, the stony heap was cast far away; / for the merit of the excavation belonging to the son whose [ditch] was wiped out was not lost.
He ascended to heaven, overjoyed through life after life, / [for the sake] of groups of his ancestral line and mothers, and of kings and friends,
and for comrades and benefactors, having dug an excavation that yields imperishable fruit, / especially for ascetics, the helpless, and Brahmins.
Indeed, having produced an excavation, one enjoys imperishable heaven. / Therefore, O Brahmins, whoever shall make an excavation and the like according to his ability,
from the destruction of all sins, would attain holy liberation—there is no doubt. / Whoever recites to people this exalted narrative of dharma,
that righteous person enjoys the fruit of donating every kind of excavation. / During an eclipse of the sun, on the excellent bank of the Bhāgīrathī,

hearing it, a person obtains the fruit of donating ten million cows; / he does not fall into poverty, nor sorrow, nor an accumulation of diseases,

Great grief does not overtake either of the two who receives disrespect.

1.58.m: Vyāsa said: / I shall explain what kind of fruit comes from all trees; / listen to that, O fortunate ones, individually in regard to planting.
He who plants auspicious trees all around upon a bank— / the holy fruit of his act cannot be fully known or told.
Whatever fruit one might obtain by planting trees elsewhere, / near water it becomes multiplied a hundred-thousandfold or ten-millionfold.
On the bank of a lotus pond itself, one enjoys infinite fruit; / therefore, we declare it a hundredfold more for those who perform the merit of [planting] trees.
Having planted an aśvattha tree in the vicinity of a reservoir of water, / what fruit a mortal gains is not [attained] even by hundreds of sacrifices.
The leaves that fall into the water on sacred days / are equal to funeral cakes here; they grant imperishable [benefit] to the ancestors.
The birds there surely eat its fruits at will; / his merit becomes imperishable, equal to feeding a Brahmin.
Indeed, the fruit that comes from the edible [produce] and planting of the aśvattha / cannot be matched even by hundreds of sacrifices, nor even by hundreds of sons.
In the heat, cows, gods, and twice-born take shelter in its shade; / and for the ancestor-groups of the planter, heaven becomes imperishable.
Because of its imperishability, no obstacle can be made for one who is healthy; / therefore, with all effort, one should plant the tree that is Mādhava.
Having planted a single tree, a man is not deprived of heaven; / therefore, O best of the twice-born, plant a great tree!
Near lovely waters, in places of buying and selling fluids, / along the road, or at a water reservoir, the magnanimous person who plants trees—
having planted the aśvattha and others, he goes to delightful heaven. / But I will declare the merit from worshipping it, O twice-born.
Having bathed, he who touches the aśvattha is released from all sins; / the mortal who touches it unbathed obtains the fruit born of bathing.
By seeing it, he destroys sin; by touching it, he attains fortune. / In circumambulating it, long life is attained. Praise be always to the aśvattha!
To the tree with rustling leaves, in which Viṣṇu is always present, / suitable for the Bodhisattva—praise be always to the aśvattha!
Having offered oblation, milk, food offerings, / flowers, incense, and a lamp to the aśvattha, one is not deprived of heaven.
Know that the worship of the aśvattha grants sons and imperishable [rewards], / increases wealth, brings renown, victory, honor, and auspiciousness.
Whatever recitation, oblation, hymn, yantra, mantra, and the like is performed / at the root of the tree with rustling leaves is declared to be multiplied ten-millionfold.
At whose root stands Viṣṇu, in the middle stands Śaṅkara, / and in the upper part stands Brahmā—who in the world would not worship it?
Whatever bath is taken silently on a Monday or a new moon day, / and in bowing to the aśvattha, has the fruit of the gift of a thousand cows.
By merely seven circumambulations, the fruit born of ten thousand cows is attained; / from abundant [circumambulations], a hundred thousand and ten million. Therefore, it should always be performed.
Whatever is given there—fruits, roots, water, and the like— / all that becomes an imperishable fruit, birth after birth.
Ah! There is none equal to the aśvattha; it is Hari in the form of a tree on earth. / Just as a twice-born is worshipful in the world, as cows, as the immortals,
so the god in the form of the aśvattha tree is remembered as most worshipful / in planting, protecting, touching, and always in ritual worship.
In turn, it bestows wealth, sons, heaven, and further, liberation. / But whatever man should cause any cutting in the trunk of the aśvattha,
having experienced hell for one kalpa, he is born among cāṇḍālas and the like. / By cutting it at the root, he attains non-return [from hell];
his ancestors remain in Raurava of terrible sight. / The fruit that arises in the planting of a single aśvattha tree
is likewise [attained] in the planting of three campaka and arka trees, / eight bilva trees, and seven nyagrodha trees,
and ten neem trees; the fruit of these is equal. / The fruit of planting each individual tree has been spoken, O twice-born.
Knowing thus, the righteous person who creates an artificial grove / [lives in heaven] for thousands of ten-million kalpas and hundreds of ten-million kalpas.
Having planted a thousand mango trees, he attains heaven; / then, by planting two- or threefold, whether less or more,
he enjoys it; having enjoyed it, he becomes a king or a virtuous lord. / Heaven to be enjoyed, then kingship, welfare, good fortune, auspiciousness,
health, and endowed with valor—all these arise simply from an orchard. / The living creatures who eat its fruits by the thousands,
the birds, insects, flying creatures, locusts, and the like that resort to it, / and the beings that resort to its shade, the diverse folk counted among them—
worshipped by the gods, they become his servants by the hundreds. / And those trees of great essence are all forms of the divine.
Their worship should be done like that of ancestors: service, water, and rice-balls. / And in the mortal realm, they become his sons birth after birth,
handsome, well-disciplined, always engaged in auspicious and virtuous deeds. / Thus creatures attached to a mango tree attain the status of leaders of the troop.
The dhātrī, the harītakī, and others producing pungent, bitter, and sour [fruits], / all of them from an orchard are pure, fruit-bearing, and ever-auspicious.
Where golden palaces are adorned with every jewel, / equipped with all ornaments, and aerial chariots swift as the wind,
trees made of gold always give everything; / charming maidens resembling Apsarases grant happiness in all seasons;
intent on song and dance, the serene givers of trees abide there. / Especially lotus ponds and whatever other excavations [there are],
fashioned within with pure stones, rivers with mud of milk-rice, / again with foam of milk, and endowed with the six tastes of food and the like—
as there is enjoyment in the mortal realm, then again in heaven, then again on earth; / again, through repetition of that, [one creates] an excavation and an orchard once more.
Just as a man becomes a lord of heaven and the mortal world by performing merit, / so a person incapable [of digging a pool] obtains the fruit of a lotus pool by erecting a water stall.
And the characteristic of a water stall here is that it removes all sins, is supreme, / grants all enjoyments, is pure, bestows heaven and liberation, and is enduring.
I shall describe the characteristics of a water stall that increase fame: / having erected a pavilion on a waterless road and in an open place,
when many travelers arrive in summer, the rainy season, and autumn, / [offering] water fragrant with agallochum and other scents, areca nuts with camphor,
a seat, and betel—having given these, one does not fall from heaven; / thus, in three years alone, one obtains the fruit of a lotus pool.
A mortal who falls from heaven is worshipped even by the gods; / whoever gives a water stall for one month in the summer in a waterless place,
dwells in heaven for one kalpa; descending from heaven, he is exalted; / those who provide water stalls dwell there where the givers of lotus pools dwell.
Otherwise, a vessel of dharma should be given, meritorious and for the destruction of sin; / this vessel of dharma is to be known as composed of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva:
'By your favor, may my desires be fruitful.' / A quarter-māṣa of gold is for the priestly gift for the vessel.
Thus, in three years alone, one obtains the fruit of giving a water stall; / whoever reads or causes to be heard the fruit arising from a lotus pool and the like,
becomes visibly freed from sin, and by that grace attains a good destination; / whoever causes this auspicious, meritorious narrative to be heard among people,
dwells in the world of the gods for thousands of crores of kalpas.

1.59.m: Vyāsa said: / 'Hereafter I shall proclaim the supreme, auspicious virtue of fame, / the holy fruit of building an embankment, as it was spoken by Brahmā.
In a forest, in impassable mud filled with stakes that injure men, / having made a causeway, a man becomes purified and attains godhood.
For a span [of path made], one attains heaven for a hundred divine years; / according to this calculated rule, a man does not fall from heaven.
If at some time, through the influence of the mud, he is born on earth from heaven, / he then becomes a glorious lord, free from disease and grief.
Having constructed bridges over mud and similar places, one does not fall from heaven; / all his sin undergoes destruction day by day.
Likewise, the fruit of causeways and bridges is proclaimed to be equal; / it is always performed by a wise man without expending life or wealth.
Listen to an ancient narrative, approved by the elders: / A certain thief, in a terrible forest, set out to commit theft.
Having placed a cow's skull in the wilderness and stepped across it, he went to steal; / having stolen the wealth of a householder,
he went to his own abode; people traversed that path, / and for all of them, there was certainly ease for one foot.
In a difficult marsh, that supreme cow's skull carried them across for one step; / and that skull situated in the forest became a Cāndrāyaṇa penance for him.
Then, upon the death of the thief, when brought before Citragupta, / this was the sole fruit of dharma that existed for him:
neither rites for the gods nor ancestral rites, nor sacred bath, nor worship of twice-borns, / nor charity, nor honor toward elders, nor knowledge, nor auspicious welfare of others.
It was not done by him even in thought, so how could it be done in deed? / Boldly, theft was committed, and the touching of another's wife,
and false accusations against living beings, and constant reviling of the virtuous; / thus a hundred thousand [sins] were done, as well as the stealing of cows.
Thereupon Dharmarāja, radiant as the fire of cosmic dissolution, said: / 'O warriors, take him to misfortune and the state from which there is no rebirth!'
At that moment, the compassionate Citragupta said: / 'He possesses a little merit from [removing] a cow's skull, O Lord; forgive him now.
Let the king obtain the rise of merit for twelve years on earth.' / Then Dharmarāja said to him: 'Go to the mortal realm, evil-minded one!
And enjoy an unobstructed kingdom for twelve years. / Because a cow's skull was removed from the path, you are released on that very account.
Having returned here again, you will go to that state from which there is no rebirth.' / Then, with joined palms, afflicted by grief, he said to the deity:
'O Dharmarāja, show compassion towards me, a sinner; / be a master to me who am masterless, as I know with affection!'
Dharmarāja then said to him: 'Very well, go from here; / deeply afflicted, you will remember your own past story through my favor.'
In the meantime, he was indeed released by the servant; / his birth took place in a certain destitute merchant family.
From birth, manifold suffering was experienced by him due to previous bad actions; / having experienced great distress for twenty-one years,
in that kingdom the king died, tormented by his own deeds. / Meanwhile, the ministers, good counselors, having deliberated,
traveled the earth with many inquiries; / and they immediately chose him firmly before everyone.
Then his royal consecration was performed by those free from envy; / and having attained the kingdom through the boon of Dharmarāja,
he constructed causeways built with stones and earth, / bridges over water-fortresses, and boats for others;
step-wells, wells, ponds, water booths, groves of trees; / and beyond this he performed diverse sacrifices and meritorious gifts.
Remembering his past deeds, for the destruction of all sins, / he practiced many kinds of dharma and various vows.
From satisfying the gods, the brāhmaṇas, and the elders, / purified of sin, he went to the abode of the wise Dharmarāja.
Then, seeing him sitting in a vehicle, his eyes became red with anger; / and with joined palms, he said to him: 'O Dharma, grant deliverance!'
Citragupta spoke these words beside Dharmarāja: / 'Purified in deed and mind, let him go to the world of Viṣṇu.'
Having heard that and having known his reason, / smiling with affection, his mind pleased, [Dharmarāja] said again: 'Go, go to the abode of Acyuta!'
A welcoming celestial chariot, variegated in color, [came] from the world of the gods; / having mounted it, he went to heaven, whence return is difficult.
Therefore, he by whom a causeway even the size of a cubit was given formerly / follows a royal lineage and goes to great heaven.
Likewise, having given pasture for cows, one is not lost from heaven; / whatever destination belongs to a giver of cows will surely be his.
By whichever wise person even a fathom of pasture for cows has been released, / heaven becomes his desired reward; what need of many other words?
He who sets aside pasture for cows according to his ability with a [pious] purpose, / his merit is more than a hundredfold [that of] feeding brāhmaṇas day by day.
Therefore, having granted pasture for cows, one is not lost from heaven; / but he who cuts down a sacred tree, or cuts off pasture for cows,
twenty-one generations of his are cooked in the Raurava hells. / The village cowherd, being capable and knowing the destroyer of cow-pasture, should punish [him];
[namely,] the cutter of trees of dharma, especially the destroyer of cow-pasture; / in punishing him lies happiness for that [cowherd], therefore he should punish him.
Whichever man builds a temple for a shrine of Viṣṇu, / three stories or five stories high, very beautiful, endowed with fine water-jars,
or whoever gives more than this, [a temple] made of clay or made of stone, / well-stocked with wealth and livelihoods, very lovely, with divine ground,
endowed with the rite of installation, surrounded by attendants and others, / a fine emblem of his chosen deity, especially of Viṣṇu—
having made it, that best of men attains complete union with Viṣṇu. / Likewise, having fashioned an image of Hari or of another [deity],
and having made a lovely shrine, whatever fruit a man obtains, / that cannot be obtained by thousands of sacrifices, gifts, vows, and the like on earth.
For thousands of crores of kalpas and hundreds of crores of kalpas, / in a palace joined with jewels and filled with abundant wealth,
he would dwell in an aerial chariot that moves at will, captivating to all the worlds; / fallen from heaven, he becomes a sovereign king, self-controlled by his virtues.
Having caused a temple to be built for a liṅga of Śiva according to his capacity— / what has been said regarding a shrine of Viṣṇu is to be known regarding the house of Śiva.
The fortunate one enjoys supreme pleasure that brings peace to the mind, / filled with delightful women, granting joy everywhere in heaven.
[He obtains] inexhaustible enjoyments on earth as a king or an exceedingly wealthy man. / Whichever man makes an image of Hara in a temple,
whether a fine liṅga or of beautiful form, dwells in heaven for a crore of kalpas; / fallen from heaven, he becomes a king, wealthy, or most venerable.
A man who makes a shrine for all the emblems of the Goddess / would attain divinity in the world of the Goddess, which gives rise to all happiness.
He abundantly attains the status of Acyuta and reaches unblemished happiness / in a temple created of jewels, with ground variegated with gems,
to be enjoyed with ten thousand lovely women, free from fear, created by the Goddess, / devoted to dance and song, charming, delighting all the senses,
rich in jeweled mardala drums and cymbals, resounded constantly by women, / spotless, delight-giving, lovely, in a very auspicious house of jewels.
Likewise, [having built] an excellent temple for an image of the Goddess, / a man goes to the heavenly realm for a million crores of kalpas.
Fallen from heaven, he becomes a king devoted to the worship of the Goddess; / and thus for a thousand births he becomes Kāmadeva himself on earth.
A man who with devotion builds a temple for Gaṇapati or for the Goddess, / having become worshipped by the hosts of gods, is born in heaven.
Likewise he attains royalty, with enjoyments in the city of the Goddess; / [he becomes] without obstacles in all undertakings, just as Gaṇapati is always.
His command is not thwarted among gods, asuras, and men; / likewise, the best of men obtains this fruit in the case of a temple to the Sun:
free from disease, very cheerful of mind, equal in splendor to Kāmadeva, / a granter of boons in all the worlds, just as the Sun indeed is.
Having made a house of stone for an image of the Sun, / and having enjoyed heaven for a hundred crores of kalpas, he becomes a lord of the earth.
Whatever separate worship there is for all the deities, beginning with Viṣṇu, / I shall proclaim each one for the benefit of human beings.
He who gives a ghee lamp day and night for one month / is worshipped by the best of gods in heaven for ten thousand divine years.
Likewise, whichever man on earth performs a bath with ghee for a liṅga, / in a single month that man obtains thousands of crores of kalpas [in heaven].
For a lamp of sesame oil or any other [substance], the fruit is half of that; / by the fruit of giving water for one month, one attains mastery.
By giving incense, one becomes a Gandharva; by sandalwood, it is doubled; / by giving the essence of musk and aloe, there is abundant reward.
By offering a garland and flowers, a man becomes a lord among gods; / by giving cotton cloth in the cold, he is freed from all suffering.
In birth after birth, it is obtained; and by giving a cooling cloth in the heat, / he who gives clothing according to his means does not falter at all.
By giving a beautiful body-covering four cubits in size / and a covering for the feet, he does not fall from heaven.
By giving gold according to one's means, a man becomes honored in heaven; / in a pavilion ten yojanas wide, he obtains beauty.
By giving gold combined with gems, he receives ten times more; / from diamonds, lapis lazuli, emeralds, rubies, and the like of priceless value,
having given them according to rule to a liṅga or to a renowned Brahmin, / he becomes the ruler over a circle a hundred yojanas wide.
Moreover, even when born on earth, he pleases all people; / by giving fragrant substances, he becomes eloquent and handsome.

By giving betel nut, a man gains a throat sweet with red nectar; / by giving an excellent maidservant, a man dwells in heaven for a kalpa.

By giving an excellent maidservant, he is born on earth as a lord of wealth; / likewise, by giving a servant, he will have many servants in heaven.
On earth, imperishable prosperity is born [for him] in birth after birth; / by giving all kinds of musical instruments, he becomes virtuous and approved by the world.
Through the science of dance, song, and the like, he becomes a lord of Gandharvas; / accompanied by maidservants and servants in heaven, he is endowed with wealth and excellent women.
Likewise, by giving a cow, he dwells in heaven for that long; / and by offering milk upon the liṅga, a man dwells in heaven for a kalpa.
By bathing [it] with curds, it is double; but with ghee, it is a hundred times more; / by giving food endowed with the six flavors, he becomes an earthly ruler.
Likewise, by giving milk-rice, he becomes the foremost of sages on earth; / having joyfully given food fit for oblations, he masters the meaning of the Veda and treatises.
And by giving meatless food, he becomes a chaste student of the Veda keeping vows; / by giving honey, molasses, and salt, [he attains] good fortune.
Charm [produced] by sugars and the like is celebrated in all the worlds; / having performed worship according to rule for the gods and for Śambhu's liṅgas,
in due order he becomes the master of the worlds beginning with heaven; / for the sake of the welfare of the worlds, the gods stand before him.
Having circumambulated Śambhu's liṅgas once, a wise person, / that best of men, goes to heaven for a full hundred divine years.
In this very manner, in due course, through prostrations to the Self-born, / praised by the world, he goes to heaven; therefore, one should practice it daily.
The man who steals the wealth of the god in the form of a liṅga, / he, having reached Raurava, becomes a worm because of that theft.
He who takes away the donor's worship meant for the liṅga and for Hari, / together with a thousand million ancestors does not turn back from hell.
Having taken wealth or other things intended for water, flowers, and lamps, / if it is not given afterward out of greed, he goes to imperishable hell.
Having stolen a maidservant of the liṅga, one does not turn back from hell; / one afflicted with lust might go to his own mother, but should not go to Śiva's servant-woman.
Having gone to a servant-woman of Śiva, and likewise by seizing the property of Śiva, / and from eating his food and drink, a man meets an evil fate.
Therefore, the priest serving the temple idol does not turn back from hell; / hence, for courtesans, wicked conduct alone would turn out beneficial.
Therefore, having touched a courtesan, a man becomes purified by bathing; / she goes to a vile, evil state because of resorting to many men.
A courtesan who is ascetic, who is always devoted to worshipping the gods, / intent on fidelity to her partner, and pure, enjoys imperishable heaven.
The one who looks upon an approaching courtesan as his mother, / godlike, enjoys all pleasure in the worlds of the gods.
Just as Hari is to be venerated by gods, asuras, and men, / so is he worthy [of worship] in all worlds, the sole purifier of all beings.
He who is always a servant of the gods, eager in divine duties, / he, as a lord of the world, goes to and is glorified in the world of the gods.
Having fashioned liṅgas of these [materials] and a pavilion / according to one's means, hear the determination of time regarding the heaven he obtains:
One year by straw, a hundred years by reed-stalks, / ten thousand by other wood, and a hundred thousand by acacia wood;
tens of millions [of years] by very firm stones joined with effort; / therefore, with all effort, a wise man should cause a pavilion to be made.
For as long a time as the maker of the pavilion dwells in heaven, / for that same time a man meets an evil fate by taking it away.
At a charming gathering of people, at the buying and selling of goods, / at a shelter for travelers, and at the confluence of rivers and streams,
the fruit a man obtains by building a pavilion for the gods, / he obtains twice that fruit [by building one] at the dwelling of a Brahmin.
Especially for a helpless, destitute person and for a learned Vedic scholar, / having caused a pleasant house to be made, a man does not fall from heaven.
Whoever constantly listens to this incomparable, meritorious narrative / attains imperishable heaven and gains the fruit of [donating] palaces and the like.
Having caused it to be recited or having recited it before the rich, the powerful, / and also before the virtuous, a man does not fall from heaven.
The Brahmin who always recites [it] to the male and female servants of the gods / and always in the temples of the gods, goes on the path to liberation.
Having recited it before kings, lords, the wealthy, and the virtuous, / he attains liberation; from hearing it, one receives that same reward.
The Brahmins said: / In the mortal world, O best of Brahmins, what is the supreme, common virtue, / easily attained, worshipped by mortals, and by sages and ascetics,
for people of the four castes and stages of life, for the sinful and the virtuous, / for those with good qualities and those without, and likewise for those with caste and those without caste?
Vyāsa said: / Among all beings, the one endowed with a rudrākṣa is superior; / by the sight of him, the mass of people's sins is dissolved.
From touching it, he enjoys heaven; from wearing it, he attains the nature of Rudra; / he who wears a rudrākṣa on his head, chest, and arms,
he is equal to Īśāna in the world, visible everywhere in sacrifice; / wherever that Brahmin stays, that region becomes meritorious.
Even by seeing or touching him, a person is purified from sin; / whatever recitation, libation, gift, bath, worship, and circumambulation,
whatever merit he performs, all that becomes endless; / and among sacred places, O Brahmins, the fruit of the rudrākṣa is the greatest sacred place.
Simply by wearing it, an embodied soul is purified from sin and possesses great merit; / and having taken an auspicious rosary endowed with the knot of Brahmā,
whatever recitation, gift, praise, mantra, and worship of gods is performed, / it all reaches imperishability, and sin goes to destruction.
We declare the characteristics of the rosary; let it be heard, O best of Brahmins! / Knowing its characteristics, you will obtain the Śaiva path.
Devoid of natural clefts, bored by insects, broken in mark, / or beads stuck together—one should avoid these in succession on a rosary.
One strung by oneself, slack, clinging to one another, / or strung by a Śūdra or the like and impure—one should avoid it from afar.
The bead placed in the middle should be repeated in proper sequence, / turning it with the hand, repeatedly touching the central meru bead.
The mantra that one recites counted [has fruit], but uncounted it is fruitless. / One should recite the mantra of all deities with their respective rosary.
Intent [in recitation] at any sacred ford, [the fruit] becomes multiplied tens of millions of times, / or upon pure ground, in a clean place, at the base of a tree,
in a cowshed, in a hall at a crossroad, reciting the mantra of Viṣṇu, Śiva, / Gaṇapati, or the Sun, one obtains endless fruit.
In a deserted house, before a corpse, in a cremation ground, or at a crossroad, / the practitioner who recites the mantra of the Goddess attains success immediately.
