Whatever non-Vedic mantra, Purāṇic, or born of the Āgamas, / all grant the desired object when recited on a rosary of rudrākṣa beads.
One should bear upon one's head the pure water streaming from a rudrākṣa. / Purified of all defilement, one's religious merit becomes imperishable.
Every single bead of a rudrākṣa has an individual immortal deity. / The mortal who wears it—I bow to him—becomes the best among the gods.
The twice-born said: / Whence was the rudrākṣa born, or whence did it attain purity? / For what purpose did it become a plant on earth, and by whom was it propagated?
Vyāsa said: / Formerly, in the Kṛta age, O brāhmaṇas, a demon named Tripura, / having slain the gods, stood indeed in an aerial city,
firm in the destruction of all worlds due to a boon from Brahmā. / Śaṅkara heard the dread report presented by the gods, O Lord.
Then, having strung the bow Ajagava and taken an arrow resembling the god of death, / having seen him with a divine eye, he slew him.
He fell upon the surface of the earth like a great meteor falling from the sky. / From Rudra, agitated by the battle, drops of sweat fell.
There, from the teardrops, the great rudrākṣa tree arose on the earth. / Living beings do not know its fruit because it is extremely secret.
Then, on the peak of Kailāsa, having bowed his head to the earth / before Maheśvara, the god of gods, Skanda spoke these words:
“O Lord, I wish to know truly the fruit of the rudrākṣa / in recitation, in wearing, or even in seeing and touching it.”
The Lord said: / A hundred thousand is the merit from seeing it, ten million indeed from touching it, / and from wearing it a man obtains a merit of a hundred million fruits.
Reciting [mantras] with it, he obtains merit measured by hundreds and thousands of millions; / there is no doubt to be entertained in this matter.
Whether impure with food remnants, engaged in forbidden acts, or united with all sins, / he is surely freed from all evils by wearing a rudrākṣa.
If even a wild beast dies with a rudrākṣa around its neck, / it too attains the state of Rudra, what then to speak of human beings and others?
Even if devoid of meditation and concentration, if one wears a rudrākṣa, / freed from all sins, one goes to the highest destination.
Kārtikeya said: / The one-faced, the two-, three-, four-, five-, and six-faced, / the seven-, eight-, and nine-faced, and the ten- and eleven-faced,
the twelve-faced rudrākṣa, and likewise the thirteen-faced, / and the one endowed with fourteen faces, spoken of as Śaṅkara himself—
which deities reside in those respective faces? Tell me that, / and what is their virtue or flaw, O Lord of the universe?
If there is favor toward me, tell it according to truth. / The Lord said: / The one-faced is Śiva directly; it wipes away the sin of killing a brāhmaṇa.
Therefore one should wear it on the body for the destruction of all sins. / He goes to Śiva's realm and rejoices together with Śiva.
Through a great conjunction of merit, by the cause of Hara's grace, / a mortal obtains a one-faced [bead] and Kailāsa, O six-faced one.
The god of gods [resides in] the two-faced; and the man who wears it, / all his sin goes to destruction, even what is hidden, such as the killing of a cow;
and he attains imperishable heaven from wearing the two-faced. / The three-faced is Fire directly; in whosever body it rests,
it burns the sin acquired throughout his lives like fire burns firewood. / From the slaying of women, the slaying of brāhmaṇas, and the slaying of many others,
whatever sin a mortal incurs, all perishes at that very moment. / Whatever fruit is in the worship of fire, in sacrificial rites, and in the oblation of clarified butter,
that fruit the wise man obtains, and he enjoys endless heaven. / The one who wears the three-faced is equal to Brahmā on earth.
It burns all accumulated misdeeds, birth after birth; / no disease occurs in his stomach, nor does he fall into debility.
He incurs no defeat, nor is his house burned by fire; / these and all other [misfortunes], including lightning, are averted.
Nothing inauspicious exists for him, through the wearing of the three-faced. / The four-faced is Brahmā himself; in whosever body it rests,
he becomes a knower of all scriptures, a twice-born foremost among knowers of the Veda, / a knower of the truth of all dharma and wealth, learned in the Smṛtis and Purāṇas.
Whatever sin is incurred in killing a human being, many living beings, or in households, / all that burns away swiftly by wearing the four-faced.
Maheśa is perpetually pleased; he becomes the master of beings. / Sadyojāta, likewise Īśāna, Tatpuruṣa, and Aghora,
and Vāmadeva—these gods reside in the five faces. / Hence the five-faced is the most abundant everywhere upon the surface of the earth.
It has the form of Rudra's own son; therefore the wise man should wear it. / For thousands of millions of kalpas and hundreds of millions of kalpas,
for so long a time, before Śiva, he is worthy of worship by gods and demons. / He becomes a universal sovereign on earth, endowed with the brilliance of Śarva in the abode of Śiva.
Therefore, with every effort, one should wear the five-faced. / Wearing the six-faced, which is Kārtikeya, on the right arm,
one is freed from sins such as killing a brāhmaṇa—there is no doubt here. / Heroic like Skanda when the end of the kalpa approaches,
he meets no defeat in this world, becoming a mine of virtues on earth. / He attains youthfulness, just like the son of the Lord of Gaurī.

A brāhmaṇa becomes revered by kings, a kṣatriya attains victory, / and the classes such as vaiśyas and śūdras are ever filled with prosperity. / To him, Gaurī becomes easily accessible, granting boons like a mother.
Then, from the strength of his arms alone, a man becomes endowed with universal brilliance, / eloquent and resolute in an assembly and in a royal gathering;
he never falls into distress, nor does defeat certainly happen to him.
All these and others come from wearing the six-faced alone. / The seven-faced is Mahāsena, and the serpent king named Ananta.
In each face of this [bead], respective serpents are established: / Ananta, Karkaṭa, Puṇḍarīka, then Takṣaka,
Viṣolbaṇa, Kārīṣa, and Śaṅkhacūḍa is the seventh. / These serpents of great power are stationed in the seven faces.
Merely by wearing this, poison does not take effect in the body, / and Hara becomes supremely pleased, just as he is with the lord of serpents.
Through his pleasure, all his sins go to destruction day by day: / the killing of a brāhmaṇa, drinking liquor, theft, and that born of violating the guru's bed—
whatever sin a mortal incurs, all perishes at that very moment. / Food resembling that of the gods he will surely obtain in the three worlds.
The eight-faced is Mahāsena, and the god Vināyaka directly. / Hear from me what merit arises merely from wearing it:
birth after birth he will not be a fool, nor afflicted by sickness, nor of ruined intellect; / for him, there will always be absence of obstacles in all undertakings.
Skill in the work of writing and dexterity in great tasks— / day after day he is capable in all undertakings and deeds.
Falsifying halves, falsifying scales, and likewise all kinds of forgery, / or if he has touched a woman with his hand for the sake of penis and belly, or a teacher's wife—
all such sins it entirely destroys; / having enjoyed imperishable heaven, liberated, he goes to the supreme state.
All these virtues come from wearing the eight-faced [bead]. / The nine-faced [bead] is declared to be Bhairava; whoever wears it on his arm,
wearing that tawny bead which bestows liberation, becomes equal in strength to me. / Even one who commits a thousand hundred-crores of killings of brahmins,
he burns them all away quickly through wearing the nine-faced [bead]. / Ever worshipped in the heavenly realm by the gods like Indra,
he resides in an excellent mansion like Śiva, a lord of Gaṇas—of this there is no doubt. / And serpents are destroyed by wearing the ten-faced [bead].
And on the eleventh face, O child, the eleven Rudras are commemorated; / let one wear it constantly in his crest-tuft; hear the meritorious fruit of that:
A thousand horse sacrifices and hundreds of crores of rituals, / and whatever fruit there is of a hundred thousand cows duly gifted—
that fruit he quickly attains from wearing the eleven-faced [bead]. / He resembles Śiva in the world; there is no rebirth for him.
Whoever wears a twelve-faced rudrākṣa on his neck, / the Sun, abiding in the twelve-faced [bead], is ever pleased with him.
Whatever fruit one enjoys having performed a cow sacrifice or a human sacrifice, / that fruit he quickly attains, and the warding off of thunderbolts and the like.
There is no fear of fire, nor does disease arise; / he enjoys acquisition of wealth and happiness as a master, never poverty.
Even if he has slain elephants, horses, men, cats, mice, and hares, / wild animals, fanged beasts, jackals, and so on, or caused them to be killed,
he is freed—of this there is no doubt—from wearing the twelve-faced [bead]. / If a thirteen-faced rudrākṣa is obtained, it is Rudra;
it should be known as most auspicious, granting the fruit of all desires. / The elixir of nectar, alchemy, and magical sandals—
all these indeed succeed for that fortunate one, O six-faced one! / Even having slain mother, father, sister, brother, or teachers,
he is freed from all sins by wearing the thirteen-faced [bead]; / he attains imperishable heaven like the god Maheśvara.
If one wears a fourteen-faced rudrākṣa, O child, / constantly on his head or on his arm, it is the lump of Śiva's energy.
What more by much speaking, described again and again? / He is constantly worshipped by the gods; it is attained through the weight of merit.
Kārtikeya said: / O Blessed One, I wish to hear the ritual assignment face by face according to the rule: / with which mantra, or how is the wearing done? Tell me.
The Lord said: / Hear, O six-faced one, in truth, face by face according to the rule: / these virtues are proclaimed indeed merely without reciting mantras.
Yet the man on earth who wears it endowed with mantras, / his virtues and greatness cannot possibly be told.
The man who, taking a rosary on his head and on his chest, walks about, / at every step attains the fruit of a horse sacrifice, not otherwise.
By wearing all the faces, he becomes equal to me. / Therefore, with every effort, my son, wear a rudrākṣa.
Whoever, having worn a rudrākṣa, dies on the earth, / he goes to my delightful city, worshipped by all the gods.
Formerly in the desert land, O child, walking along on the land for trade, / a merchant's son, my dear, was tormented on a tree by a female ghost.
Then the female ghost danced repeatedly, and she was seen by a supreme twice-born: / "Who are you, dancing, miserable, wrapped in worn-out clothing?"
Then she said to the twice-born: "I heard from a messenger of the gods / that right now, through the fall of a thunderbolt on this handsome man,
death is certain, O brahmin; and he will become my husband." / Meanwhile, from the sky a thunderbolt onto his head
fell; he fell down upon the earth onto half a piece of a rudrākṣa. / Then from my city, O son, a celestial aerial vehicle swiftly descended.
Having mounted it, the glorious one then stayed there for a very long time; / having attained a portion of me, he became a master, a lord of treasure.
Such is the good destiny of one who dies even upon a piece of a rudrākṣa, O son; / the fruit of a man wearing it with knowledge, we are not able to describe.
Whether he be a Śaiva, a Śākta, a Gāṇapatya, or a Saura, / he who when dead wears a rosary or even a single rudrākṣa,
or whoever reads this, causes it to be read, recites it, or listens to it, / with soul liberated from all sin, gradually attains happiness and heaven.
